title: Shared Foundation
subtitle: Stage 0 — everyone starts here
description: The same ground floor under all seven paths. Every path below assumes it. If you are already a working engineer, skim it and move on; if you are not, this is where the first few months go.

stages.title: Programming Fundamentals
stages.description: Python syntax, OOP, file and error handling.
stages.overview: Everything else on this site assumes you can read and write a program. Python is the language used throughout, chosen because it is readable and because most AI tooling is written in it. This stage covers the language itself: storing data, making decisions, repeating work, and organising code so it can be changed later without breaking.

topics.definition: Python uses indentation rather than braces to show which lines belong together, so layout is part of the language rather than a matter of style. A program runs top to bottom, and most lines either store a value or do something with one. Getting comfortable reading that shape matters more at the start than memorising any particular command.

Every value has a type: whole numbers, decimals, text, true/false, and collections such as lists and dictionaries. The type decides what you can do with a value — you can add numbers, join text, and get an error if you confuse the two. A large share of early bugs are a value being a different type than you assumed.

Operators are the symbols that combine values: arithmetic, comparison, and the logical and, or and not. Comparison operators produce true or false, which is what conditions are built from. The one to watch is a single `=`, which assigns a value, against `==`, which tests whether two are equal.

`if`, `elif` and `else` let a program take different actions depending on a condition. This is where a program stops being a fixed list of steps and starts responding to its input. Keep conditions readable, because deeply nested ones are where logic errors hide most comfortably.

Loops repeat work: `for` runs once per item in a collection, `while` repeats until a condition stops being true. Almost anything involving more than one item uses one. A `while` loop whose condition never becomes false is the classic way to hang a program.

A function is a named, reusable block that takes inputs and usually returns a result. They exist so you can write a piece of logic once, give it a name, and use it in several places. Small functions that do one thing are markedly easier to test and to fix than long ones that do five.

A comprehension builds a list or dictionary in a single expression rather than a loop that appends to an empty one. It is shorter and, once familiar, easier to read for straightforward transformations. Use an ordinary loop when the logic needs more than one condition or step.

Reading and writing files is how a program works with data that outlives it. Use the `with` form to open them, because it closes the file automatically even if something fails partway through. Text and binary files are handled differently, and mixing them up is a common early error.

When something goes wrong Python raises an exception, which stops the program unless you catch it. `try` and `except` let you handle the failures you anticipated — a missing file, a refused connection — and let everything else surface. Catching everything and ignoring it hides bugs that will return later in a worse form.

A module is a file of Python you can use from another file, and `import` is how you reach it. This is how programs get split into manageable pieces and how you use libraries other people wrote. Understanding where Python looks for modules explains most import errors you will hit.

A class bundles data together with the functions that act on it, and an object is one particular instance of that class. It is one way of organising code among several, and it is worth knowing because most libraries you will use are built this way. You need to read it fluently long before you need to design with it.

A virtual environment is a private copy of Python for one project, so its dependencies cannot clash with another project's. Without them, two projects needing different versions of the same library cannot coexist on one machine. Create one per project without exception — it is the most useful habit in this stage.

Debugging is finding out what a program is actually doing rather than what you assumed it was doing. Printing values is a legitimate start; a debugger that pauses execution and lets you inspect variables is faster. Read errors from the bottom up — the last line names the problem, the lines above show how it was reached.

Type hints annotate what a function expects and what it gives back. Python does not enforce them while running, but your editor and checking tools use them to catch mistakes before you run anything at all. On anything larger than a short script they pay for themselves quickly.

Reading about programming does not make you able to do it; that only comes from writing code, getting it wrong and fixing it. Work through small exercises until the basics are automatic and you are no longer looking up syntax. Time spent practising here has the highest return of anywhere on this site.

stages.title: Developer Essentials
stages.overview: Writing code is only part of the job; the rest is the environment around it. This stage covers working in a terminal, keeping each project's dependencies apart, handling configuration and secrets, and reading an error message properly. These are the things nobody teaches explicitly and everybody is assumed to already know.

topics.definition: The terminal is a text interface for running programs and moving around your computer. Most development tools are driven from it, and a good number have no other interface at all. You need a handful of commands — list, change directory, copy, move, remove — not fluency in shell scripting.

A path is how you locate a file. Absolute paths start from the root of the drive; relative paths start from wherever the program happens to be running. Most “file not found” errors are a relative path being interpreted from a directory you did not expect.

`pip` downloads and installs libraries from the Python Package Index so you do not have to write everything yourself. Install into an activated virtual environment rather than system-wide. Note that the name you install is sometimes not the name you import, which catches people out regularly.

A virtual environment is a self-contained Python for a single project. You create it, activate it, and install into it; when it is active your terminal prompt usually says so. Forgetting to activate it before installing is the most common reason a package appears to vanish.

This file lists your project's dependencies so anyone can recreate the same environment with one command. Pin versions rather than leaving them open, or a fresh install months later pulls different libraries and behaves differently. It is what makes a project reproducible on somebody else's machine.

Environment variables are values handed to a program by its surroundings rather than written into it — an API key, a database address, whether this is production. They let identical code run in different places with different settings. They are also how secrets stay out of your source code.

A `.env` file holds environment variables for local development so you do not set them by hand each time. It must never be committed: add it to `.gitignore` immediately, and commit a `.env.example` listing the names with no values. A key leaked into a repository is billed to you until somebody notices.

JSON is a text format for structured data — objects with named fields, arrays, strings, numbers and booleans. It is what nearly every web API sends and receives, including every AI provider. You need to read it comfortably and to know that it maps almost directly onto Python dictionaries and lists.

YAML is another structured data format, used mostly for configuration: Docker Compose files, CI pipelines, deployment settings. It is easier to read than JSON and far more sensitive to indentation. When a YAML file will not parse, the cause is almost always whitespace.

An error message is the most useful information you will be given, and it is routinely skipped. Read the last line first, because it names the error and what went wrong. The lines above it are the traceback, showing the path through the code that led there.

Logging records what a program did while it was running. It is better than printing because you can set levels — debug, info, warning, error — and turn the detail up or down without editing code. Once something runs on a server rather than in front of you, logs are all you have.

A predictable layout — source in one place, tests in another, configuration at the root — makes a project navigable to anyone, including you in six months. Following the common convention matters more than which convention you follow. It also makes imports behave, which is otherwise a recurring annoyance.

The README is the first thing anyone opens. It should say what the project does, how to install it, how to run it, and what configuration it needs. Writing it early clarifies your own thinking, and it is the difference between a repository somebody can use and one they cannot.

Running the project on your own machine — a server on localhost, reloading as you edit — is where nearly all your time goes. Getting a fast, reliable loop in place early repays itself constantly. If it is slow or flaky you will avoid testing, and the bugs will reach production instead.

stages.title: Networking & Server Basics
stages.overview: Every application you build here is a program on one machine talking to a program on another. This stage covers how that conversation works: addresses, ports, requests and responses, and what the numbers in an error actually mean. Without it, deployment and API problems are impossible to reason about and can only be guessed at.

topics.definition: The client asks and the server answers. Your browser or your Python script is a client; the machine hosting an API is a server. Every AI call you make is this relationship, and a good deal of confusion clears up as soon as you are certain which side you are writing.

`localhost` is your own machine talking to itself, and it always resolves to the same address. When you run a development server, this is where it lives. Nothing on localhost is reachable from anywhere else, which is precisely why it is safe to develop against.

On localhost you are the only user, everything is nearby, and nothing needs securing. A deployed server is reachable by anyone, has real network latency, and holds real data. Code that has only ever run on localhost has usually never had its assumptions tested.

Binding a server to `127.0.0.1` accepts connections from your machine only. Binding to `0.0.0.0` accepts them on every network interface, which is what you need inside Docker or on a real server. This single line is why a service that works locally is unreachable once containerised.

An IP address identifies a machine on a network so that traffic can find it. Some are public and reachable from the internet; others are private and meaningful only inside one network. You will meet them constantly in configuration, firewall rules and logs.

A domain name is a human-readable label standing in for an IP address, because people remember names and not numbers. It also means the address behind it can change without anyone having to notice. Owning one is what makes a deployed application feel like a product rather than an experiment.

DNS is the system that translates a domain name into an IP address, consulted on every request. Changes take time to spread because results are cached at several levels along the way. “It works for me but not for you” shortly after a change is nearly always DNS.

One machine runs many services, and the port number says which one a request is meant for. Some are conventional — 80 for HTTP, 443 for HTTPS — while development servers commonly use 3000, 5000 or 8000. Two programs cannot listen on the same port, which is what “address already in use” means.

HTTP is the protocol browsers and APIs use to exchange messages. HTTPS is the same protocol encrypted, so nobody between you and the server can read or alter what passes. Anything carrying credentials or personal data must use it, which in practice means everything.

A request carries a method, a path, headers and sometimes a body. The response carries a status code, headers and usually a body. Every API call in every path on this site is one of these exchanges, so being able to picture both halves is worth the time it takes.

The method states intent: GET retrieves, POST creates, PUT and PATCH update, DELETE removes. Following the convention makes your API predictable to anyone who has used another one. GET in particular must not change anything, because browsers and proxies will repeat it freely.

The status code summarises the outcome: 2xx worked, 3xx look elsewhere, 4xx the caller made a mistake, 5xx the server did. The difference between 4xx and 5xx tells you immediately whose problem it is. The ones you will meet most are 401, 403, 404, 429 and 500.

TCP guarantees that data arrives, in order, retrying as necessary; UDP simply sends it and accepts that some will be lost. HTTP runs on TCP, which is why your API calls do not arrive scrambled. UDP is for video, games and anything where arriving late is worse than arriving incomplete.

SSH gives you an encrypted terminal on a remote machine, which is how servers are administered. Use key pairs rather than passwords: a private key stays on your machine, a public key goes on the server. It is also how you push to Git over SSH rather than HTTPS.

Connecting means naming a user, a host and a key; the server checks your key against the ones it trusts and drops you into a shell. From that point you are working on that machine much as if it were your own. Understanding this makes deployment feel like ordinary work rather than something mysterious.

stages.title: APIs, Backend & Databases
stages.overview: An API is how one program offers its capabilities to another, and a database is where the results are kept. This stage covers building both: defining endpoints, handling requests, storing and querying data, and doing it without leaving the door open. Nearly every path on this site is, structurally, an API in front of a model with a database behind it.

topics.definition: An API is a defined way for one program to use another's capabilities without knowing how they work inside. When you call a model provider you are using theirs; when you build a backend you are offering your own. It is essentially a contract: given this request, expect this response.

REST is the usual convention for HTTP APIs: resources have URLs, and HTTP methods say what to do with them. It is a set of conventions rather than a strict standard, which is why implementations differ in the details. Following it makes your API predictable to anyone who has used another.

An endpoint is one URL your API responds to, usually paired with a method — `GET /users` and `POST /users` are different endpoints on the same path. Each has its own inputs, outputs and rules. Designing an API is largely the work of deciding what the endpoints should be.

The request is what the client sends: a method, a path, headers, and often a JSON body. The response is what comes back: a status code, headers, and usually JSON. Being able to inspect both is how an API problem gets debugged in minutes rather than hours.

Path parameters are values embedded in the URL itself, as in `/users/42`, and they identify which resource you mean. Because they are part of the address they are always required. Use them for identity, not for options.

Query parameters follow a `?` in the URL and usually modify a request rather than identify a resource — filtering, sorting, paging. They are optional by nature and need sensible defaults. Never put anything secret in one; they end up in server logs and browser history.

JSON is the format nearly every API uses for request and response bodies. It maps almost directly onto Python dictionaries and lists, which is why working with APIs in Python feels natural. Set the `Content-Type` header correctly, or the other side may not parse what you sent.

The status code summarises the outcome: 2xx worked, 3xx look elsewhere, 4xx the caller made a mistake, 5xx the server did. The difference between 4xx and 5xx tells you immediately whose problem it is. The ones you will meet most are 401, 403, 404, 429 and 500.

Authentication answers who you are, usually with an API key, a token or a session. Every AI provider requires it, which is why you were issued a key. Send credentials in headers rather than in the URL, and never commit them to a repository.

Authorization answers what you are allowed to do, which is a separate question from who you are. A logged-in user is not automatically permitted to read another user's records. Check permissions on the server for every request — hiding a button in the interface is not a control.

A framework such as FastAPI or Express handles the repetitive parts of serving HTTP — routing, parsing, validation, documentation — so that you write the logic. Learning one well transfers to the others, because the concepts are shared. FastAPI appears throughout this site because it is Python and validates input by default.

A database stores data so that it survives your program restarting, and lets you query it efficiently. Files are fine until you need to search, update safely, or have several things writing at once. Almost every application you build will have one behind it.

A relational database stores data in tables of rows and columns, with relationships between tables expressed through shared keys. That structure is enforced, which prevents entire categories of inconsistent data. PostgreSQL is the usual default and will handle nearly anything you need.

SQL is the language for querying relational databases, and it is declarative: you describe the result you want rather than how to fetch it. `SELECT`, `WHERE`, `JOIN` and `GROUP BY` cover most day-to-day work. Learn it directly rather than only through a library that generates it for you.

Create, read, update and delete are the four things you do to stored data, and they map onto both SQL statements and HTTP methods. Nearly every backend feature is some combination of them. Recognising that pattern makes an unfamiliar codebase much faster to read.

These are the four SQL statements behind CRUD. The dangerous detail is that `UPDATE` and `DELETE` without a `WHERE` clause apply to every row in the table. Test the `WHERE` with a `SELECT` first, and take a backup before running either by hand against real data.

Your backend connects using a driver and a connection string containing host, port, database, user and password. Opening a connection is expensive, so applications keep a pool of them open and reuse them. Keep that string in an environment variable, never in the code.

Documentation is what makes an API usable by anyone who did not write it, including you in six months. It should state each endpoint, its inputs, its outputs and its errors. Generated documentation stays accurate as the code changes; handwritten documentation drifts almost immediately.

OpenAPI is a standard format for describing an HTTP API in a machine-readable way. From that description you get interactive documentation, generated client libraries and request validation without extra work. FastAPI produces it automatically from your code, which is much of why it is recommended here.

The essentials are: HTTPS everywhere, authenticate every endpoint that is not deliberately public, validate all input, rate limit, and never return internal error details to a caller. Most breaches exploit a missing basic rather than anything sophisticated. The OWASP list is the standard checklist and is worth reading through once properly.

stages.title: Developer Tools
stages.description: Git, GitHub, Docker, Postman, VS Code.
stages.overview: These are the tools you will have open every day. Git and GitHub track and share your work, Docker packages it so it runs the same anywhere, and the rest let you inspect an API, a database or a running page instead of guessing at it. Learning them properly once saves time on every project afterwards.

topics.definition: VS Code is the editor most of this ecosystem uses, and it is free. Its real value is the extensions: Python support, Git integration, Docker, and inline error checking as you type. Learn the command palette and the integrated terminal early, because they remove most of the friction.

Git records the history of your project so you can see what changed, undo mistakes, and work on several things at once. It is the most important tool in this stage and repays learning properly rather than memorising four commands. Commit small, coherent changes with messages that explain why.

GitHub hosts Git repositories and adds collaboration around them — issues, pull requests, review, automation. It is also, in practice, your public portfolio: the projects in each path are meant to end up here. Employers do look at it.

A graphical Git client, useful while the command line is still unfamiliar. Seeing changes and history laid out visually makes the underlying model considerably easier to grasp. Move to the command line eventually, because that is what every tutorial and CI system assumes.

Postman lets you send HTTP requests by hand and inspect exactly what comes back. It is how you test an endpoint without writing client code, and how you establish whether a bug is in your request or in their server. Saved collections double as informal documentation for a team.

An SSH client with saved connections and stored keys, so reaching a server is one click rather than a remembered command. It is a convenience rather than a necessity — the `ssh` command does the same job. It becomes worth it once you are managing more than one machine.

Docker packages an application together with its dependencies so it runs identically anywhere. It removes the whole class of failure where code works on your machine but not on the server. For Python and AI work, where library versions are notoriously brittle, this matters more than for most software.

Built into the browser, DevTools show the page structure, the console, and every network request with its headers and response. For anything touching the frontend it is where problems get diagnosed. The network tab in particular is the quickest way to see what your code actually sent.

A database client that connects to almost anything and lets you browse tables and run queries in a window. It is far quicker than a terminal client for finding your way around an unfamiliar schema. Check which environment you are connected to before running anything that writes.

The dedicated administration tool for PostgreSQL, covering queries, schema, users and server settings. It exposes more Postgres-specific detail than a general-purpose client does. Use it when you are administering a Postgres server rather than only querying one.

Notebooks run code in cells and show the output — including charts — inline, which suits exploring data and trying things out. Most AI and ML tutorials are written as notebooks, so you will read them constantly. They are for exploration: move code into ordinary files before it becomes something you maintain.

Copilot suggests code as you type, based on the surrounding context. It is genuinely useful for boilerplate and genuinely confident when it is wrong, so read every suggestion before accepting it. While you are learning, be careful it does not quietly do the thinking you are meant to be practising.
